title: Signal · Tuesday 3 November
overview: Goldman Sachs limits AI coding tools to engineers, Swiss cantonal banks warn against a FINMA 'mega authority', and Anthropic's amended filing says it may imminently meet its AI-acceleration threshold.

top.headline: Goldman limits Claude Code and GitHub to engineers, barring most traders and bankers
top.summary: Goldman Sachs has barred most of its traders and bankers from AI coding tools, including Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub, according to Bloomberg as reported by Quartz and PYMNTS. Internal guidance updated in October limits the tools to engineers; the strats who combine engineering, research and trading are not covered. Goldman said it assesses productivity and risk, then gives tools to the staff best suited to them.
top.why: A bank that had championed front-office coding has pulled back, so private banks running similar pilots can expect risk and compliance to ask who owns the code and the controls.
top.background: In July, chief information officer Marco Argenti spoke favourably of vibe coding by non-technical staff, who passed their work to one of the firm's 12,000 engineers.
top.watch_next: Whether others follow: JPMorgan has said outside AI agents will not be allowed inside the bank, and Bank of America is limiting agents' access to consumer deposits.

top.headline: Cantonal banks warn FINMA package would create a 'mega authority'; FINMA rejects the charge
top.summary: Oliver Buschan, director of the Association of Swiss Cantonal Banks, says the Federal Council's draft reads largely like a FINMA wish list and warns of a 'mega authority with great potential for arbitrariness' (translated from German), according to finews, citing the NZZ am Sonntag. The package, in consultation until 19 November, includes a senior managers regime, wider early intervention powers and fines of up to 10 percent of annual operating income.
top.why: Documented accountability would reach most mid-sized Swiss banks, which could put a named senior manager behind data, model and outsourcing decisions.
top.background: The regime would cover banks with more than 250 staff, which the association says means 19 of 24 cantonal banks. FINMA says the powers follow the parliamentary inquiry's recommendations on Credit Suisse and that serious breaches 'should not be free' (translated from German).
top.watch_next: The Federal Council plans its message to parliament in 2027, and a decision may come only after the autumn 2027 elections.

top.headline: Update: Anthropic's amended filing says it may imminently meet its AI-acceleration safety threshold
top.summary: Anthropic's amended S-1, filed on 2 November, adds a risk factor saying internal estimates on future models indicate it 'may imminently meet' its Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI', according to TechCrunch, which quotes the filing. It says no current model exceeds that threshold, and that it has in the past not identified a significant acceleration until after it occurred.
top.why: Banks using frontier models rely on vendor assessments, and this filing says capabilities may advance faster than safety and validation work. TechCrunch notes an S-1 is both disclosure and marketing.
top.background: TechCrunch reads this as a warning about recursive self-improvement, where AI substantially speeds up its own development. Anthropic says it does not expect to safely use Claude to build later frontier models fully autonomously and is considering policy updates to keep humans in control.
top.watch_next: Any change to the Responsible Scaling Policy, and further amendments to the filing before the listing.

items.headline: Bitcoin Suisse CEO says Switzerland has lost interest in crypto as jobs move abroad
items.summary: Andrej Majcen told news agency AWP that Switzerland no longer ranks among the top countries in the firm's review of crypto adoption and regulation. Bitcoin Suisse is cutting 60 of 120 Swiss jobs, as announced in September, and moving back-office work to Bratislava, where some wage costs are 60 to 70 percent lower.
items.why: A pillar of Crypto Valley now focuses on wealth management for institutions and wealthy clients, which brings it closer to private banks' digital asset offers.

items.headline: FCA review of wholesale banks lists AI kill-switch, inventory and oversight weaknesses
items.summary: The FCA published supervisory findings on 2 November. AI concerns include insufficient human oversight, unapproved tools causing data leakage, inadequate kill switches and incomplete AI inventories. It also cites data ingestion defects and an algorithm change that caused a significant unintended intraday position, according to Regulation Tomorrow.
items.why: Gives banks with London desks a supervisor's checklist for AI controls, and it sits alongside Goldman's decision on coding tools.

items.headline: Eurex Clearing calls itself first hybrid CCP as ESM digital bond qualifies for repo
items.summary: Eurex Clearing said native digital instruments, including issues by the European Stability Mechanism, will trade in Eurex Repo's GC Pooling segment, clear under one rulebook and risk model, and count as margin collateral. The ESM's EUR 1 billion digital bond settled on 2 November via Clearstream's D7 and the Eurosystem's Pontes, according to Ledger Insights.
items.why: Banks could reach digital collateral through existing clearing relationships, with no new connectivity or legal agreements, which lowers the entry cost for European tokenised markets.

items.headline: Santander puts AI's business value at EUR 194 million for nine months
items.summary: Banco Santander reported on 28 October that AI generated EUR 194 million in the first nine months of 2026, up from EUR 35 million in the first quarter, according to Startup Fortune. It counts extra revenue, lower costs and lower loan-loss provisions. The bank targets more than EUR 1 billion across 2026 to 2028, with tools for all 185,000 staff.
items.why: A published euro figure, with its definition, gives boards at other European banks a number to ask about.

items.headline: Broadridge plans on-chain voting and transfer agency for NYSE's tokenised platform
items.summary: Broadridge said on 2 November it plans to bring on-chain shareholder governance and digital transfer agency services to the NYSE's tokenised securities platform, due to launch after regulatory approval. NYSE will use Broadridge's smart contracts to connect tokenised shares to meeting agendas, voting rules and verifiable results.
items.why: Custodians and wealth platforms would have to carry shareholder rights on tokenised stock, which adds corporate actions to any tokenisation plan.

items.headline: BNP Paribas creates a Swiss investment banking unit under Christoph-Sebastian Meier
items.summary: BNP Paribas said Christoph-Sebastian Meier took over its new Investment Banking Switzerland unit on 2 November, leading it from Zurich with a focus on advisory, according to finews. Meier has 20 years in M&A, ten of them at Lincoln International. The unit will serve corporate, financial institutions and wealth management clients.
items.why: It follows last week's securities services appointment in Switzerland and points BNP Paribas at advisory work for Swiss corporates and wealth clients.

items.headline: Euronext to nominate NN Group's David Knibbe as CEO as Boujnah leaves in 2027
items.summary: Euronext said on 2 November it intends to nominate David Knibbe, chief executive of NN Group since 2019, at its annual general meeting on 20 May 2027. Stéphane Boujnah, in post since 2015, steps down in May 2027. NN Group said Tjeerd Bosklopper becomes chief executive designate on 1 March and succeeds Knibbe after its 12 May meeting.
items.why: A leader from a regulated industry, chosen for integration and technology experience, takes over as Europe moves to T+1 settlement in October 2027.

items.headline: Italy weighs a 26 percent exit levy on wealthy residents, media reports say
items.summary: Giorgia Meloni's government could impose a 26 percent capital gains levy on people who move tax residence abroad with assets above EUR 800,000, according to media reports cited by WealthBriefing. Marc Acheson of insurance-wealth firm Utmost said it could penalise those who relocated in good faith under the flat-tax regime, now EUR 300,000 a year.
items.why: Swiss booking centres with Italian clients would face new planning questions, and the idea tests the flat-tax model that drew wealth to Italy.

items.headline: BNP Paribas Wealth Management plans more growth in Germany after HSBC deal
items.summary: Vincent Lecomte, chief executive of BNP Paribas Wealth Management, told WealthBriefing the purchase of HSBC Private Bank's German business more than doubled its size there, to 50 billion of assets under management and fourth place among private banks. He said the bank wants to invest further, with 10 German cities covered.
items.why: Shows a European bank buying scale in German entrepreneur and family wealth, and promising to add more.

items.headline: OpenAI lifts critical bug bounties more than fourfold ahead of its next security sprint
items.summary: OpenAI said on 2 November that researchers from Cathedral will join its next internal security sprint, using OpenAI models to test its defences. Critical bounties on core products rise to as much as USD 30,000, with exceptional findings eligible for up to USD 172,000 including bonuses, according to RuntimeWire.
items.why: Gives bank vendor reviews a concrete request for AI suppliers: evidence of outside testing and of what it found.

items.headline: Chainalysis says attackers used offensive agentic techniques to breach its systems
items.summary: Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said an outside actor used 'offensive agentic techniques' to reach its systems and internal tools, according to SecurityWeek. User IDs, names, email addresses and role labels were accessed; it says investigation content, query results and credentials were not. The firm says it sees an industry-wide rise in AI-driven attacks.
items.why: A vendor to financial institutions and law enforcement now reports an agent-led intrusion, which adds AI-driven attacks to third-party risk reviews.

items.headline: Palantir's US commercial revenue passes government for the first time, up 148 percent
items.summary: Palantir reported third-quarter revenue of USD 2.31 billion on 2 November, up 96 percent. US commercial revenue rose 148 percent to USD 984 million, ahead of USD 953 million from the US government. It raised full-year guidance to about USD 8.53 billion; the shares fell about 3 percent after hours, according to Stocktwits on Yahoo Finance.
items.why: Large companies are paying for AI and data operations at scale, which will feature in banks' build-or-buy debates.

items.headline: New York Times sues Brave, naming Anthropic and others as buyers of scraped content
items.summary: The New York Times sued Brave in federal court in Manhattan on 2 November, alleging it scraped copyrighted content and distributed it to customers the suit names as Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI and Cohere, according to TechCrunch. The Daily News, Chicago Tribune and Orlando Sentinel filed a similar suit. The Times seeks an injunction and damages.
items.why: Legal exposure now reaches the data suppliers behind AI models, so bank procurement may start asking how search and grounding data is licensed.

items.headline: Databricks makes Lakebase Postgres generally available on Google Cloud
items.summary: Databricks said on 2 November that Lakebase, its fully managed serverless Postgres database, is generally available on Google Cloud, with autoscaling, scale to zero, instant branching and point-in-time recovery. It shares a storage layer with analytics data, so apps and agents run on one governance model with no separate pipelines.
items.why: Banks on Google Cloud gain a transactional store inside the Databricks governance model, useful for agents that need both live and analytical data.
items.for_your_skills: Architecture & TOM can now offer Lakebase on Google Cloud as a managed option for agent state and operational data.

say_it_today: Goldman has taken coding agents back from its traders just as the FCA lists unapproved tools, weak kill switches and incomplete AI inventories among its concerns at wholesale banks. The useful question for any bank this week is which AI tools can run code, under whose permissions, and who signs off the result.
